blocuri.text: The document says what happened in the real world. Accounting needs the same information in a specific form: which account is debited, which account is credited, and for what amount. The translation between the two is called a journal entry, and this chapter shows what it looks like.

The good news for a business owner: they don't have to do the translation themselves. The useful news: it's worth knowing how to read it, because it's the only place where you can check whether the software — or the accountant — has correctly understood the document.
Anatomy of an Entry
A journal entry has five elements, none of them superfluous.

blocuri.titlu: What a journal entry is made of
randuri: when the transaction occurred — not when you record it
what happened, in words, for whoever reads it years later
blocuri.nota: The transaction date and the recording date can differ; in accounting, the first one counts.

blocuri.text: The short form, used by everyone in the profession, puts the debit account before the credit account, separated by an equals sign: 371 = 401 means "goods came in, the payable to the supplier increased." It's read from left to right: what we obtained, where it came from.
An Invoice, Three Lines
The most common document in a company's life, the purchase invoice for goods with VAT, produces a three-line entry. Let's take an invoice for 1,000 lei plus 210 VAT, totaling 1,210.

randuri: the goods entered the warehouse, at their cost
the tax paid to the supplier, which you will deduct
this is the total you owe
blocuri.nota: A single account credited, two debited. The sum of the debits equals the credit: 1,000 + 210 = 1,210.

blocuri.text: This shows why VAT is neither goods nor an expense. The 210 lei cost the company nothing: it will be deducted from the VAT payable. That's why it sits in its own account, separate from the value of the goods — and if the company were not VAT-registered, the 210 would be added to the cost of the goods, because it would remain there permanently.
The same document produces different entries depending on the company's tax regime. The document is the same; its accounting is not.
Simple Entry and Compound Entry

When the transaction links a single account to a single account, the entry is simple: collection from a customer, 5121 = 4111. When one of the two sides splits into several accounts, as in the invoice above, the entry is compound.

What is not allowed, though it may seem convenient, is an entry with multiple accounts on both sides at once, mixing unrelated transactions. Such an entry balances on the total, but it can no longer be read: a year later, no one can say which amount on the left corresponds to which amount on the right.
The Preview: How to Check Without Knowing Accounting

Here lies, for a business owner, the most useful habit in the entire book. Before saving a document, the software shows exactly what entry it will write. You don't need to know the formula to do the check; you just need to look at three things.

blocuri.titlu: What to check in the preview
randuri: is it the one on the paper in your hand?
does it describe what actually happened?
"goods" when you bought goods, "services" when you bought a service?
blocuri.nota: Accounts have names in ordinary language precisely so that this check is possible without accounting training.

blocuri.text: A detail that seems technical but is important: the preview must come from the same engine that produces the actual entry. If the software calculates the preview in one place and the entry in another, the two can silently drift apart, and what you checked is no longer what was saved.

Account correspondence is not arbitrary: it follows from the function of each account and the nature of the transaction, and entries that do not respect normal correspondences — for example, crediting an expense account outside of a reversal or closing — almost always signal a misclassification, not an exotic situation. The compound entry is acceptable; the "mixed" one, with multiple accounts on both sides, should be avoided: it loses the traceability of the correspondence, complicates the account ledger, and makes line-by-line verification impossible during an audit. The date that matters for recording is that of the transaction, not that of the document nor that of entry into the software — the distinction becomes critical at period boundaries, where an invoice dated the 30th of the month but received on the 5th belongs to the month in which delivery occurred, affecting VAT chargeability. Finally, the entry's explanation is not decoration: when reconstructing an old transaction, it is often the only element linking an amount to an economic fact, especially after the attached document has migrated between systems.
Who Does the Translation

In practice, no one composes entries by hand for ordinary documents. The software has the translation ready for each typical situation: you choose which document you have, fill in the amounts from it, and the entry composes itself.
This set of ready-made translations is called a chart of accounting treatments (monografie), and its richness determines how often you need to improvise. That's the subject of the next chapter.
The Same Document, Translated Differently at Three Companies

The same piece of paper does not produce the same entry at every company. It's worth seeing in a case, because it clarifies what actually determines the translation: not the document, but WHAT the company does with what it bought.

blocuri.titlu: A 10,000-lei Invoice for a Laptop, at Three Companies
randuri: uses it for over a year, above the threshold
goes in as a part of a product
blocuri.nota: The document is identical in all three. What differs is the purpose, and the company knows the purpose, not the supplier.

blocuri.text: From this follows a surprising consequence: the accountant cannot make the translation alone, from the document, for every transaction. For ordinary ones, the pattern is clear. For ambiguous ones, information is needed that is written nowhere — and the question asked then is cheaper than the correction made a year later.

enunt: Invoice from a supplier: base 4,000 lei, VAT 21% = 840 lei, total 4,840 lei, for "maintenance materials." The company will consume them this month.
Write the complete journal entry and say what changes if the company is NOT registered for VAT purposes.
rezolvare: VAT-registered company, two lines: 302 Consumable materials = 401 Suppliers, 4,000 lei; 4426 Deductible VAT = 401 Suppliers, 840 lei. Total payable to the supplier: 4,840.
Upon actual consumption, a third transaction, with a different document (consumption slip): 602 = 302, 4,000 lei.
Company NOT registered for VAT: the tax cannot be deducted, so it enters the COST of the item. A single line: 302 = 401, 4,840 lei. There is no 4426 account in the entry.

The practical consequence, often ignored: for a non-VAT-registered company, the VAT on received invoices is not a recoverable tax, but part of the price. Comparisons between offers from a VAT-registered company and a non-registered one must therefore be made on different amounts.

puncte: A journal entry has five elements: the transaction date, the explanation, the debit account, the credit account, the amount.
It's read from left to right: what we obtained, where it came from. 371 = 401 means goods received on credit.
Deductible VAT is neither goods nor an expense: it's a receivable from the state, which is why it has its own account.
The same document produces different entries depending on the company's tax regime — for a non-VAT-registered company, the tax becomes part of the cost of the item.
The preview can be checked without accounting knowledge: the amount, the explanation, the account names.
The date that matters is that of the transaction, not that of entry into the software.
